title: Small Self-Portrait Planting a Tree

image.credit: Photograph via Wikimedia Commons (ShiTaoMaster Shi Planting Pines.jpg)

source.label: Wikipedia: Shitao moved “to Anhui in the 1660s”; the self-portrait is dated c. 1674

highlight.text: Nevertheless, much of his art is focused upon gardens and flowers, and in his well-known self-portrait he presents the image of himself instructing a young boy and a monkey in the planting of pine trees in his garden.

source.author: Richard M. Barnhart
source.title: Peach Blossom Spring: Gardens and Flowers in Chinese Paintings
source.publisher: The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Internet Archive scan)

source.label: Sirén: “The composition is in the form of a short handscroll”
Sirén: “the trees and rocks with richer ink”

work.text: The painter, who is wearing his long white [summer] gown, sits on a stone at the root of a beautiful [pine] tree [occupied] in supervising [the] transportation of smaller trees for planting, [the] work being performed by a [servant-boy] and a creature which looks more like an anthropoid than a [human] being.

source.author: Osvald Sirén
source.title: Chinese Painting: Leading Masters and Principles, vol. V

moment.text: During early Qing times, Buddhism was seriously split between Ming loyalist and pro-Qing factions. Young Shitao was spurned by the loyalist camp … In becoming a disciple of Lu’an Benyue, the dispossessed former Ming prince found himself squarely in the pro-Manchu camp.

source.author: Wen C. Fong
source.title: Wang Hui and Repossessing the Past
source.publisher: in Maxwell K. Hearn (ed.), Landscapes Clear and Radiant: The Art of Wang Hui (1632–1717), The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Internet Archive scan)

moment.text: In the cases of Pa-ta-shan-jen, [Shih-t’ao], and K'un-ts'an, their assumed monk's names alone witness their chosen path of retreat from the world.

source.author: Sherman E. Lee
source.title: Chinese Landscape Painting
source.publisher: The Cleveland Museum of Art (Internet Archive scan)

matters.text: [Through this the situation] gets a touch of humour, though the [extraordinary] being is [not] meant to amuse anybody; the master [himself] seems indeed [to] be [filled] with melancholy thoughts as he watches the [performance].

source.author: Osvald Sirén
source.title: Chinese Painting: Leading Masters and Principles, vol. V

matters.text: Shitao’s life and art, therefore, necessitated the reimposition of order, or reintegration, through a lifetime of chaos and struggle.

source.author: Wen C. Fong
source.title: Wang Hui and Repossessing the Past
source.publisher: in Maxwell K. Hearn (ed.), Landscapes Clear and Radiant: The Art of Wang Hui (1632–1717), The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Internet Archive scan)

medium: handscroll; ink and color on paper
